title: 10 Strongest Animals on Earth (Pound for Pound) | Wild Rank

segments.text: When we think of strength, we picture elephants, bears and gorillas. But strength is relative. If you compare how much an animal can lift, pull or crush against its own body weight, the ranking flips upside down, and some of the champions are smaller than a grain of rice. Today we are ranking the ten strongest animals on Earth, pound for pound. Stay until number one, because the winner is an animal most people have never even heard of.

segments.name: Tiger
segments.text: Number ten: the tiger. The largest cat on the planet is built like a spring. Its front legs and shoulders are packed with muscle, which lets it bring down prey such as deer and wild cattle. After a kill, a tiger will often drag the carcass into cover, and that prey can weigh more than the tiger itself. In raw power, few land predators come close. But pound for pound, the tiger is only getting started on this list.

segments.name: Gorilla
segments.stat: Several times stronger than a human
segments.text: Number nine: the gorilla. A large male silverback can weigh around twice as much as an adult man, and almost all of that is muscle. Estimates of exactly how strong gorillas are vary a lot, and many viral numbers are exaggerated, but scientists agree they are several times stronger than a human. They can snap thick bamboo and tear apart vegetation with ease. Despite that power, gorillas are mostly calm, gentle plant eaters.

segments.name: Elephant
segments.text: Number eight: the elephant. The African elephant is the largest land animal alive. Its trunk has no bones at all, yet it is controlled by tens of thousands of muscle units, giving it both strength and precision. An elephant can use its trunk to lift loads of hundreds of kilograms, push over trees and carry logs, and the same trunk can pick up a single peanut. In total strength it beats everything on land. Pound for pound, though, smaller animals are about to take over.

segments.name: Harpy Eagle
segments.stat: Talons longer than a grizzly's claws
segments.text: Number seven: the harpy eagle. Living in the rainforests of Central and South America, it hunts monkeys and sloths that it snatches straight from the treetops. Its back talons can be longer than the claws of a grizzly bear, and its grip is among the most powerful of any bird. Lifting heavy, struggling prey off a branch and flying away with it takes enormous strength for an animal that weighs less than a house cat.

segments.name: Leafcutter Ant
segments.stat: Carries loads many times its weight
segments.text: Number six: the leafcutter ant. These ants cut pieces of leaves and carry them back to their nest, often over long distances, in columns of thousands. Each worker hauls a fragment many times heavier than its own body, and it does it all day long. The leaves are not food for the ants directly. They use them to grow a fungus garden, which is what the colony actually eats. Endurance and strength combined.

segments.name: Weaver Ant
segments.text: Number five: the Asian weaver ant. Weaver ants build nests by pulling leaves together and gluing them with silk, forming living chains with their bodies. Their grip is extraordinary. One famous photograph shows a weaver ant hanging upside down from a smooth surface while holding an object around one hundred times its own weight. Imagine a person hanging from a ceiling by their hands while holding a small truck.

segments.name: Coconut Crab
segments.text: Number four: the coconut crab, the largest land invertebrate in the world. As its name suggests, it can crack open coconuts. In 2016, Japanese researchers measured its claws and found a pinching force of over three thousand newtons. That is stronger than the grip of almost any other animal they compared, and it rivals the bite of some big predators. All of that power comes from an animal that weighs only a few kilograms.

segments.name: Rhinoceros Beetle
segments.text: Number three: the rhinoceros beetle. Named for the horn on the males' heads, these beetles use it to wrestle rivals. Their strength has been tested in the lab. In one study, rhinoceros beetles walked while carrying up to thirty times their body weight, and they could support loads of around one hundred times their weight. For a human, that would mean holding up the weight of several cars.

segments.name: Horned Dung Beetle
segments.text: Number two: the horned dung beetle. These small beetles live in tunnels beneath piles of dung, where males fight to keep rivals out. In a 2004 study, scientists measured how hard a male could pull, and the result was astonishing: one thousand one hundred and forty-one times its own body weight. For an average person, that would be like pulling six double-decker buses full of people. For years, this was considered the strongest insect on the planet.

segments.name: Oribatid Mite
segments.text: And number one: the oribatid mite. This tiny creature, smaller than a millimeter, lives in soil and moss all over the world, so small that you have almost certainly walked past millions of them. In 2007, researchers glued tiny weights to one species and found it could hold about one thousand one hundred and eighty times its own body weight. Relative to its size, it is one of the strongest animals ever measured. Proof that in nature, size is not everything.

Which one surprised you the most? Let us know in the comments. If you enjoyed this ranking, subscribe to Wild Rank, because next time we are ranking the most dangerous bites in the animal kingdom, and number one might not be the animal you expect.

description:
Strength is relative. When you compare power to body weight, the ranking of the strongest animals on Earth flips upside down. From tigers and elephants to beetles and a mite smaller than a millimeter, here are the 10 strongest animals pound for pound.
